title: Canadian novelist removed from Prix Goncourt longlist after AI allegations

reading.body:
This is a case of contested authorship resolved by a prize committee rather than by a court or a technical authority. The failure sits at the point where a published literary work enters a competition, and the question asked of it is whether a human wrote it. The Académie Goncourt acted on allegations and on its own review, and the removal is an administrative decision about eligibility, not a finding that AI wrote the book.

The detection claim rests on a single tool, Pangram, reported to have scored the novel at 100 per cent AI. A detector score is a probabilistic output, and the summary gives no indication that it was validated against this text, this author, or French-language fiction generally. The publisher that could have checked, Les Editions du Boréal, said it could not determine whether AI was used before the manuscript arrived, which places the gap at acquisition, the last point at which a publisher could have asked for drafts, process records or an explanation of how the text was produced.

Catching this earlier would have required evidence of composition rather than a classifier's verdict, since a score cannot distinguish generated text from text a detector misreads. What is not established is whether Orélien used AI at all, whether the plagiarism examples amount to plagiarism, and whether Pangram's score is accurate for this novel. The AI claims were rejected by the author and his French publisher, and an allegation is not a finding.

reports.title: Canadian novelist removed from Prix Goncourt longlist after AI allegations

summary:
The Prix Goncourt removed Canadian author Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était ça ou mourir from its longlist after reviewing allegations that he used AI to write it. The Académie Goncourt also said his earlier work appeared to contain plagiarism, citing examples reported by Montreal newspaper La Presse. The prize will be awarded in early November. Orélien and his French publisher, Éditions Grasset, had rejected the AI claims, which followed a post saying the detector Pangram gave the novel a 100 per cent AI score.

His Quebec publisher, Les Editions du Boréal, paused promotion but said it could not determine whether AI was used before the manuscript arrived. The novel had sold to 23 countries and was set for English publication by Scribner in 2028. Orélien, who lives in Ottawa, told Libération he was angry and did not need a machine to write. A University of Toronto professor, Kevin Bryan, said the book was clearly AI-written and offered $1,000 to anyone who could prove Pangram falsely flags human French texts.
